title: Chidambaram Questions India's BRICS Gains; BJP Calls It 'Disgruntled Uncle' Attitude
excerpt: P. Chidambaram said the last two or three BRICS summits delivered no tangible benefits for India. BJP leader Ram Madhav fired back with a "naraz phupha" jibe as the 2026 New Delhi summit approaches.
body:
• Former Union minister P. Chidambaram questioned the "tangible benefits" India has drawn from BRICS meetings, saying the last two or three summits delivered no concrete gains for New Delhi.
  • The remarks came ahead of the 2026 BRICS Summit, which India is set to chair in New Delhi, and drew a swift and sharp BJP counterattack.
  • Senior BJP leader Ram Madhav called the Congress leader's stance a "naraz phupha" (disgruntled uncle) attitude, asking why nobody questioned the benefits when the UPA government hosted BRICS summits.
  • BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari accused the Congress of suffering from FOMO over India hosting the summit, turning the chairmanship year into a political flashpoint.

Congress leader and former Union minister P. Chidambaram has questioned what India has actually gained from its engagement with BRICS, saying the last two or three summits of the grouping produced no tangible benefits for New Delhi. The remarks, made in the run-up to the 2026 BRICS Summit that India is set to chair in the capital, drew an immediate and combative response from the BJP — and turned the country's chairmanship year into a fresh political battlefield.

Chidambaram's core contention was blunt: "I didn't see any benefits," he said, asking what concrete gains India had secured from recent BRICS meetings. The comment landed at a delicate moment, with New Delhi preparing to host the grouping and shape its agenda.

The spark

The argument flared into the open at India Today's BRICS Roundtable 2026, where the session titled "Sangh, Shakti, Samvad: India's Voice in the BRICS Order" examined India's evolving role within the bloc. Speaking there, senior BJP leader Ram Madhav launched a full-throated rebuttal of Chidambaram, borrowing a phrase from Prime Minister Narendra Modi's own lexicon.

https://x.com/CNNnews18/status/2097895347553018361

"Inhi ko PM (Modi) calls naraz phupha. When the UPA hosted BRICS summits, did anybody say what the benefit of it was?"

— Ram Madhav, senior BJP leader

Madhav, the BJP's national vice president, argued that India's growing global influence was unsettling the opposition. "To dismiss these forums as having no relevance is a complete lack of understanding of the contemporary global reality," he said, according to India Today, adding that a new world order was on the horizon and India would have to play a balanced role in it.

The BJP's pushback did not stop there. Party spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari accused the Congress of behaving like an "angry uncle" and suffering from FOMO — fear of missing out — now that India is hosting the summit. Another line of attack came from the BJP's broader camp, which asked what the Congress had achieved diplomatically since 1947.

Context: India's BRICS chairmanship

BRICS — originally Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, and since expanded — has grown from an acronym coined by economists into a standing forum of major emerging economies. India is no stranger to hosting it: New Delhi hosted summits in 2012 and 2016, and chaired the bloc again in 2021.

That is the backdrop against which Chidambaram's question lands. His scepticism is not new — Congress leaders have long argued that multilateral photo-ops substitute for outcomes — but posing it in the chairmanship year guarantees it will be read as a political intervention, not merely a policy critique.

Analysis: an old argument, new stakes

Strip away the rhetoric and the dispute is about how India measures the returns of multilateral diplomacy. Chidambaram's camp argues the summits have produced declarations more than deliverables — that for all the joint statements, India cannot point to a trade deal or an institutional win that traces directly to a BRICS table.

"To dismiss these forums as having no relevance is a complete lack of understanding of the contemporary global reality. It is surprising to have come from someone who served as foreign minister."

— Ram Madhav, senior BJP leader

The BJP's counter is that influence is cumulative and structural: hosting and shaping a bloc that now spans much of the Global South builds the diplomatic capital India draws on in every other forum, from the G20 to bilateral trade talks. Madhav's point — that nobody asked about benefits when the Congress itself hosted BRICS — is designed to paint the criticism as opportunistic rather than principled.

Both arguments have a constituency. India's foreign policy establishment has generally treated BRICS as a useful hedge — a place to engage Russia and China while projecting leadership across the developing world. Whether that hedge pays in measurable returns is a fair question; whether the chairmanship year is the moment to ask it is the political one.

The diaspora angle

For Indians abroad, the spat matters because BRICS increasingly frames the economic weather they live under — remittance corridors, energy prices and the investment climate back home all show up in an NRI household's budget. A chairmanship year means India will visibly set an agenda; diaspora communities across the Gulf, Southeast Asia and Africa sit inside BRICS' expanding footprint and will feel its policy ripples first.

What's next

The immediate watchpoint is the summit itself: what New Delhi puts on the agenda, and whether the outcomes carry anything the sceptics would recognise as a tangible gain. Politically, the "naraz phupha" line is likely to echo through the season, with the BJP casting Congress as grudging about India's global moment and the Congress pressing its case that pageantry is not policy.
nri_angle: BRICS debates shape trade, energy and investment conditions that directly affect NRI households, and India's 2026 chairmanship puts New Delhi's agenda-setting in the spotlight for the diaspora.
